claim: Fly wings are innervated by two major sensory nerves that navigate along the L1 vein and along the L3 vein.
source: Fly wings are innervated by two major sensory nerves that navigate along the so-called L1 vein located at the anterior margin (L1 nerve) and along the L3 vein (L3 nerve) (Figure 1a–d).
evidence: This is a direct statement in the text describing the anatomical structure of fly wings.

claim: Glial cells originating from the sensory organ precursors present on the anterior margin migrate proximally toward the central nervous system following the axon bundle.
source: Glial cells originating from the sensory organ precursors (SOPs) present on the anterior margin migrate proximally, i.e. toward the central nervous system (CNS) following the axon bundle and ensheathing it throughout its length.
evidence: This is a direct description of glial cell migration behavior in the manuscript.

claim: L1 glia initiate migration at around 18 hr After Puparium Formation.
source: L1 glia initiate migration at around 18 hr After Puparium Formation (hAPF), reach the level of the Costal nerve at around 22–24 hAPF and join the glial cells on the Radius by 28 hAPF.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of migration initiation based on observations.

claim: L1 glia reach the level of the Costal nerve at around 22–24 hAPF.
source: L1 glia initiate migration at around 18 hr After Puparium Formation (hAPF), reach the level of the Costal nerve at around 22–24 hAPF and join the glial cells on the Radius by 28 hAPF.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of migration progress based on observations.

claim: L1 glia join the glial cells on the Radius by 28 hAPF.
source: L1 glia initiate migration at around 18 hr After Puparium Formation (hAPF), reach the level of the Costal nerve at around 22–24 hAPF and join the glial cells on the Radius by 28 hAPF.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of migration completion based on observations.

claim: The migratory process has been subdivided into three steps: 'Initiation', 'Costa reach' and 'Complete migration'.
source: The migratory process has been accordingly subdivided into three steps: 'Initiation', 'Costa reach' and 'Complete migration' (Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the authors categorized the migration process.

claim: Fra is detected in glia at the time these cells begin to move.
source: Fra is detected in glia at the time these cells begin to move as well as in the underlying axons (Figure 1e–g'', Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c, g).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by immunolabeling data shown in figures.

claim: Fra is detected in the underlying axons.
source: Fra is detected in glia at the time these cells begin to move as well as in the underlying axons (Figure 1e–g'', Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c, g).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by immunolabeling data shown in figures.

claim: The Fra protein seems to be evenly distributed along the L1 glial chain.
source: The Fra protein seems to be evenly distributed along the L1 glial chain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–g).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on observations shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Fra levels are considerably reduced in the glia and in the surrounding cells within the fra knock down clones.
source: The WT clones covering glia along the L1 nerve and surrounding cells show expression of Fra (GFP-expressing cells in Figure 1k–k'''), whereas Fra levels are considerably reduced in the glia and in the surrounding cells within the KD clones (RFP expressing cells in Figure 1j–j''').
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by CoinFLP clone analysis shown in figures.

claim: Migrating glial cells of the peripheral nervous system express Fra.
source: Thus, migrating glial cells of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) express Fra.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Fra expression data presented.

claim: fra3 heterozygous wings show incomplete L1 glia migration in a significant fraction of samples.
source: We first focused on the most characterized loss-of-function (LOF) allele fra3 (Kolodziej et al., 1996). As this mutation is embryonic lethal in homozygous conditions, we analyzed fra3 heterozygous wings and found incomplete L1 glia migration in a significant fraction of samples, as shown by the position of the glial nuclei (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype observed in fra3 heterozygous mutants, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The number of glial cells is not affected in fra3 heterozygous wings and hence cannot be the cause of the migratory defect.
source: The number of glial cells is not affected and hence cannot be the cause of the migratory defect (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a direct statement based on quantification shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Wings heterozygous for fra3 and carrying the >GFP transgene show incomplete glia migration as shown by the position of glial GFP labeling.
source: To test this possibility, we assessed the migratory index of glial cells labelled by the >GFP transgene, which allowed us to visualize glial processes in flies that were heterozygous for the .. These wings also show incomplete glia migration as shown by the position of glial GFP labeling (Figure 2e–g)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype observed when visualizing glial processes, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Glial cells require Fra to complete their migration.
source: These wings also show incomplete glia migration as shown by the position of glial GFP labeling (Figure 2e–g) suggesting that glial cells require Fra to complete their migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fra mutants show incomplete migration.

claim: The Fra receptor is expressed in glial cells and is seemingly necessary for their efficient migration.
source: In summary, the Fra receptor is expressed in glial cells and is seemingly necessary for their efficient migration.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the Fra expression and loss-of-function data presented.

claim: The knock down of fra using the gcm>GFP driver reveals a significant decrease in migration efficiency as compared to that observed in the control wings.
source: The knock down of fra using the gcm>GFP driver, which is the earliest glial driver, reveals a significant decrease in migration efficiency as compared to that observed in the control wings (Figure 3a, compare blank and light blue columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype observed upon fra knockdown, supported by data in Figure 3a.

claim: Wings that express the UAS-fra-RNAi together with the UAS-fra transgene show complete rescue of the migratory phenotype induced by the fra KD.
source: To exclude the possibility of off-target effects, we analyzed wings that express the UAS-fra-RNAi together with the UAS-fra transgene, and found complete rescue of the migratory phenotype induced by the fra KD (Figure 3a, patterned light and dark blue column).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue experiment, supported by data in Figure 3a.

claim: The RNAi line induces a specific phenotype and fra acts in a cell autonomous manner.
source: This strongly suggests that the RNAi line induces a specific phenotype and that fra acts in a cell autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiment showing specificity of the RNAi effect.

claim: Reintroducing fra expression only in the glial cells of fra3/+ animals rescues the migratory phenotype, albeit partially.
source: Finally, as a complementary approach, we reintroduced fra expression only in the glial cells of fra3/+ animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), and found that this rescues the migratory phenotype, albeit partially.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a rescue experiment, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The lack of total rescue in fra3/+ animals with glial fra expression may be ascribed to the neuronal requirement of Fra.
source: Given the high levels of Fra expression in the gcm>fra GOF wings (Figure 3g–g''''), it is unlikely that this partial rescue is due to suboptimal levels of Fra. Rather, the lack of total rescue may be ascribed to the neuronal requirement of Fra.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of partial rescue and Fra expression in neurons.

claim: Around one third of fra3/+ wings show an axonal navigation phenotype.
source: Figure 1e–f''''' shows that Fra is expressed in glia as well as in neurons, and indeed around one third of fra3/+ wings show an axonal navigation phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the frequency of axonal navigation defects, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In fra3/+ wings with axonal navigation phenotype, axonal navigation is delayed, which may indirectly affect glial migration.
source: In these wings, axonal navigation is delayed, which may indirectly affect glial migration.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential indirect effect of axonal defects on glial migration.

claim: nsyb-driven expression starts to be detected around 18 hAPF but the expression is more prominent at 22 hAPF and onwards.
source: nsyb-driven expression starts to be detected around 18 hAPF; but the expression is more prominent at 22 hAPF and onwards (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f–h").
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal expression pattern of nsyb-Gal4, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knocking down fra specifically in neurons using nsyb-Gal4 shows no delayed glia migration except in one third of the wings which present an axonal navigation defect.
source: We then knocked down fra specifically in neurons using nsyb-Gal4 and found no delayed glia migration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1i), except in one third of the wings, which present an axonal navigation defect (not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype observed upon neuronal fra knockdown, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Axon navigation defects indirectly affect glia migration.
source: This is in line with the above-mentioned fra3/+ data and with previous data showing that axon navigation defects indirectly affect glia migration (Giangrande et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fra acts in a cell autonomous manner in glial cells to mediate migration.
source: In summary, we find that acts in a cell autonomous manner in glial cells to mediate migration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the cell-specific knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Levels of Fra are critical for the initiation stage of glial cell migration.
source: Furthermore, our data show that that levels of Fra are critical for the initiation stage of glial cell migration and that this is mediated through the cytoplasmic domain of Fra.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the dose-dependent effects of Fra on migration initiation.

claim: Fra-mediated migration is mediated through the cytoplasmic domain of Fra.
source: Furthermore, our data show that that levels of Fra are critical for the initiation stage of glial cell migration and that this is mediated through the cytoplasmic domain of Fra.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dominant negative experiment with the cytoplasmic domain deletion construct.

claim: The migratory phenotype of fra3/+ glia that also carry the gcm>GFP driver is much stronger than that of fra3/+ glia.
source: Interestingly, the migratory phenotype of fra3/+ glia that also carry the gcm>GFP driver is much stronger than that of fra3/+ glia (compare Figure 2e patterned black an gray column, MI = 67% and Figure 4a patterned light gray and white column, MI = 14%).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of migratory indices between two genotypes, supported by data in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The phenotype is further enhanced in glia that express both the gcm>GFP and a gcm RNAi line.
source: The phenotype is further enhanced in glia that express both the gcm>GFP and a gcm RNAi line (Figure 4a patterned brown and pink column).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the enhanced phenotype, supported by data in Figure 4a.

claim: The gcm-Gal4 driver is a hypomorphic gcm allele that results from the insertion of a Gal4-containing transposon into the gcm promoter.
source: Since the gcm-Gal4 driver is a hypomorphic gcm allele that results from the insertion of a Gal4-containing transposon into the gcm promoter (Jacques et al., 2009), the above result raised the possibility that Gcm and Fra interact genetically.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the nature of the gcm-Gal4 driver, supported by citation.

claim: Gcm and Fra interact genetically.
source: Since the gcm-Gal4 driver is a hypomorphic gcm allele that results from the insertion of a Gal4-containing transposon into the gcm promoter (Jacques et al., 2009), the above result raised the possibility that Gcm and Fra interact genetically.
evidence: This is a hypothesis raised based on the observation that gcm-Gal4 enhances the fra phenotype.

claim: Reducing the dose of Gcm enhances the fra3-mediated phenotype.
source: To explore this possibility, we analyzed the glia migration phenotype in double heterozygous conditions for fra and two other gcm hypomorphic alleles, including the gcmrA87 enhancer trap carrying a LacZ transposon inserted into the gcm promoter and the imprecise excision line gcm (Riabinina et al., 2015; Vincent et al., 1996; Jacques et al., 2009). In addition, we also used a gcm null mutation, gcmN7-4 (Bernardoni et al., 1997). This confirms that reducing the dose of Gcm enhances the fra3-mediated phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genetic interaction, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b and citations.

claim: Crossing the fra3 mutation with a gcm driver that does not affect the gcm locus does not show the enhanced migratory phenotype present in the fra3, gcm-Gal4 wings.
source: Furthermore, we crossed the fra3 mutation with a gcm driver that does not affect the gcm locus, a transgenic line carrying 6Kb of the gcm promoter fused to the Gal4 gene, which is inserted on the third chromosome (Flici et al., 2014). In these wings, we did not observe the enhanced migratory phenotype present in the fra3 , gcm-Gal4 wings (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a control experiment, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and citation.

claim: The two genes fra and gcm act in the same genetic pathway that impinges on glial cell migration.
source: These findings suggest that the two genes act in the same genetic pathway that impinges on glial cell migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Gcm is a transiently expressed transcription factor that acts very early in glial differentiation.
source: Gcm is a transiently expressed transcription factor that acts very early in glial differentiation (Hosoya et al., 1995; Vincent et al., 1996; Jones et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Gcm's role, supported by citations.

claim: The gcm RNA becomes detectable by 8–9 hAPF in wild-type wings.
source: In situ hybridization on wild-type (WT) wings has shown that the gcm RNA becomes detectable by 8–9 hAPF (Van de Bor and Giangrande, unpublished data) and fades in glial cells by 24 hAPF (Popkova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about gcm expression timing, supported by unpublished data and citation.

claim: The gcm RNA fades in glial cells by 24 hAPF.
source: In situ hybridization on wild-type (WT) wings has shown that the gcm RNA becomes detectable by 8–9 hAPF (Van de Bor and Giangrande, unpublished data) and fades in glial cells by 24 hAPF (Popkova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about gcm expression timing, supported by citation.

claim: Migration is less efficient when the amount of Gcm is reduced.
source: Three allelic conditions were tested: gcm-Gal4/gcmrA87(gcm LOF) (Figure 4a, light brown column, MI = 63%, vs. the MI = 90% of the control line gcm>GFP/+ (white column)), gcm-Gal4 homozygous (Figure 4a, orange column, MI = 41%) and gcmrA87/gcmN7-4 transheterozygous (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, last column, MI = 28%) animals. Migration is indeed less efficient when the amount of Gcm is reduced and the MI is restored to normal values upon reintroduction of Gcm expression (Figure 4a, patterned pink columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the effect of Gcm reduction on migration, supported by data in Figure 4a and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The MI is restored to normal values upon reintroduction of Gcm expression in gcm mutants.
source: Migration is indeed less efficient when the amount of Gcm is reduced and the MI is restored to normal values upon reintroduction of Gcm expression (Figure 4a, patterned pink columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue of the gcm phenotype, supported by data in Figure 4a.

claim: Using the UAS-gcm-RNAi line to reduce the amount of Gcm results in a migratory defect.
source: Finally, we used the UAS-gcm-RNAi line to reduce the amount of Gcm (gcm KD) and also observed a migratory defect (Figure 4a, dark brown column, MI = 25%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype of gcm knockdown, supported by data in Figure 4a.

claim: Overexpressing Fra in gcm KD wings rescues the migratory phenotype indicating that gcm plays a regulatory role in migration and that the RNAi effects are specific.
source: The rescue obtained upon co-expressing the UAS-gcm and the UAS-gcm-RNAi transgenes indicates that gcm plays a regulatory role in migration and that the RNAi effects are specific (Figure 4a, patterned pink-dark brown column).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue experiment, supported by data in Figure 4a.

claim: Overexpressing Gcm using the UAS-gcm transgene is sufficient to increase the migration efficiency of glial cells.
source: Furthermore, overexpressing Gcm using the UAS-gcm transgene (gcm GOF) is sufficient to increase the migration efficiency of glial cells, as the percentage of wings showing complete migration increases compared to that in control animals (Figure 4a, pink column and Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the gain-of-function phenotype, supported by data in Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: Migration starts later in Gcm LOF wings compared to that observed in control wings.
source: To determine which migratory step is affected by Gcm, we analyzed the gcm LOF (gcm>GFP/gcmrA87) and the gcm GOF (gcm>GFP/+;UAS-gcm/+) wings by confocal time-lapse microscopy and found that migration starts later in Gcm LOF and earlier in gcm GOF wings compared to that observed in control wings (Figure 4c–f).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of migration initiation in gcm mutants, supported by time-lapse data in Figure 4c-f.

claim: Migration starts earlier in gcm GOF wings compared to that observed in control wings.
source: To determine which migratory step is affected by Gcm, we analyzed the gcm LOF (gcm>GFP/gcmrA87) and the gcm GOF (gcm>GFP/+;UAS-gcm/+) wings by confocal time-lapse microscopy and found that migration starts later in Gcm LOF and earlier in gcm GOF wings compared to that observed in control wings (Figure 4c–f).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of migration initiation in gcm overexpression, supported by time-lapse data in Figure 4c-f.

claim: Gcm affects the initiation of glial cell migration in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Thus, Gcm affects the initiation of glial cell migration, like Fra, and it does so in a dose-dependent manner: gcm GOF enhances the efficiency of this step and gcm LOF lowers it.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the dose-dependent effects of Gcm on migration initiation.

claim: The levels of Gcm and Fra are crucial for the initiation of glia migration.
source: In summary, the levels of Gcm and Fra are crucial for the initiation of glia migration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the dose-dependent effects of both Gcm and Fra on migration initiation.

claim: Only a minor fraction of gcm KD wings contains converted cells and only a few cells are converted into neurons.
source: We inspected the rate of glia to neuron conversion in gcm KD wings by using the anti-Elav antibody, which specifically recognizes neurons at the analyzed stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–b'' gcm KD). Only a minor fraction of the wings contains converted cells and only a few cells are converted into neurons, strongly suggesting that fate conversion is not the cause of the altered MI (on average, 14% of the gcm KD wings show up to 10 Repo/Elav double-positive cells along the L1 nerve, >15 wings were analyzed per genotype; none were observed in wild-type wings).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the frequency of fate conversion, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fate conversion is not the cause of the altered MI in gcm KD wings.
source: Only a minor fraction of the wings contains converted cells and only a few cells are converted into neurons, strongly suggesting that fate conversion is not the cause of the altered MI (on average, 14% of the gcm KD wings show up to 10 Repo/Elav double-positive cells along the L1 nerve, >15 wings were analyzed per genotype; none were observed in wild-type wings).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the low frequency of fate conversion in gcm KD wings.

claim: gcm KD wings that do not show Repo/Elav positive cells still show a strong delay in migration.
source: In addition, we restrained our analysis to gcm KD wings that do not show Repo/Elav positive cells and still found a strong delay in migration (MI = 45%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the migration phenotype in gcm KD wings without fate conversion.

claim: The glial migration phenotype observed in gcm mutant animals is not due to its early requirement in glial cell determination, but specific to cell migration.
source: These data strongly suggest that the glial migration phenotype observed in gcm mutant animals is not due to its early requirement in glial cell determination, but specific to cell migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of fate conversion and migration in gcm mutants.

claim: The number of Repo-positive cells in gcm LOF and KD backgrounds is lower than that in the wild-type glial chain.
source: The number of Repo-positive cells in gcm LOF and KD backgrounds is indeed lower than that in the wild-type glial chain and, accordingly, gcm GOF wings contain supernumerary glial cells (Figure 5a, light brown, dark brown and pink columns, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct statement about glial cell number in gcm mutants, supported by data in Figure 5a.

claim: gcm GOF wings contain supernumerary glial cells.
source: The number of Repo-positive cells in gcm LOF and KD backgrounds is indeed lower than that in the wild-type glial chain and, accordingly, gcm GOF wings contain supernumerary glial cells (Figure 5a, light brown, dark brown and pink columns, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct statement about glial cell number in gcm overexpression, supported by data in Figure 5a.

claim: Overexpressing String or Dacapo in glia induces a significant change in glial cell number compared to that present in control wings.
source: First, we produced animals overexpressing String or Dacapo in glia (gcm>GFP) and verified that this induces a significant change in glial cell number compared to that present in control wings (Figure 5a, compare white column with columns with vertical and horizontal lines).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the effect of cell cycle regulators on glial cell number, supported by data in Figure 5a.

claim: Migration efficiency is not affected by overexpressing String or Dacapo in glia.
source: Then, we analyzed the migration efficiency in both backgrounds and found that it is not affected (Figure 5b), even though the glial number increase induced by String overexpression and the decrease induced by Dacapo overexpression are comparable to those observed in gcm GOF and LOF, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of effect of cell number changes on migration, supported by data in Figure 5b.

claim: Defective glia migration is found even in gcm KD wings containing a wild-type number of glial cells.
source: Finally, we found defective glia migration even in gcm KD wings containing a wild-type number of glial cells, in agreement with the above data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the migration phenotype independent of cell number, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The absolute number of glia does not affect migration efficiency.
source: Thus, the absolute number of glia does not affect migration efficiency, further corroborating the hypothesis that Gcm specifically affects this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell number manipulation experiments.

claim: gcm is expressed in hemocytes.
source: It is already known that gcm is also expressed in hemocytes (Bernardoni et al., 1997; Bataillé et al., 2005; Waltzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement about gcm expression, supported by citations.

claim: Knocking down gcm in hemocytes using collagen-Gal4 shows no defect in glia migration.
source: To clarify this, we used an independent hemocyte driver, collagen-Gal4, which is expressed in the embryonic hemocytes (Asha et al., 2003). We knocked downgcm in hemocytes (collagen-Gal4 crossed with the UAS-gcm-RNAi) and found no defect in glia migration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of effect of hemocyte gcm knockdown on glia migration, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d and citation.

claim: Gcm is only present embryonically in blood cells.
source: Furthermore, as Gcm is only present embryonically in blood cells,we used a gcm-Gal4, tubulin-Gal80thermosensitive(ts) line to specifically knock down fra in glia after embryogenesis and confirmed that, in these conditions too, glia migration is affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal expression of Gcm in blood cells, supported by a temporal control experiment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Fra and Gcm act cell autonomously in glial cells to control migration on the developing wing disc.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Fra and Gcm act cell autonomously in glial cells to control migration on the developing wing disc.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the cell-specific knockdown experiments.

claim: A DAM ID screen suggests that Gcm may directly control the expression of genes involved in glia migration, including fra.
source: A DNA adenine methyltranferase identification (DAM ID) screen aimed at identifying the direct targets of Gcm does indeed suggest that this potent transcription factor may directly control the expression of genes involved in glia migration, including fra (Cattenoz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the DAM ID screen results, supported by citation.

claim: There are three canonical Gcm-binding sites in the fra locus, two of which are located at the position of a strong DAM ID peak.
source: There are three canonical Gcm-binding sites (GBS) in the fra locus, two of which are located at the position of a strong DAM ID peak, which is indicative of Gcm binding (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genomic analysis of fra, supported by data in Figure 6a.

claim: qRT PCR assays show an increase in the GFP levels upon co-transfection of the fra reporter vector with the Gcm expression vector and this effect is dose dependent.
source: qRT PCR assays clearly show an increase in the GFP levels upon co-transfection of the reporter vector with the Gcm expression vector and this effect is dose dependent (Figure 6b, columns with a red color gradient).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cell transfection assay results, supported by data in Figure 6b.

claim: Gcm-dependent activation of the fra reporter is completely abolished upon mutagenesis of the two GBSs.
source: To further demonstrate that the effect of Gcm on fra is direct (Figure 6a''), we showed that Gcm-dependent activation of the reporter is completely abolished upon mutagenesis of the two GBSs (Figure 6b, columns with a yellow color gradient).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the mutagenesis experiment, supported by data in Figure 6b.

claim: Fra levels are reduced in gcm KD wings compared to control wings.
source: Finally, we complemented the in vitro data with two in vivo assays. First, we showed that Fra levels are affected in opposite direction in gcm LOF and GOF wings (Figure 6c–f).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Fra protein levels in gcm mutants, supported by data in Figure 6c-f.

claim: Fra levels are increased in gcm GOF wings compared to control wings.
source: Finally, we complemented the in vitro data with two in vivo assays. First, we showed that Fra levels are affected in opposite direction in gcm LOF and GOF wings (Figure 6c–f).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Fra protein levels in gcm overexpression, supported by data in Figure 6c-f.

claim: In gcm GOF wings, the levels of the Fra protein already increase by 15 hAPF, in agreement with the observed precocious initiation of migration.
source: In gcm GOF wings, the levels of the Fra protein already increase by 15 hAPF, in agreement with the observed precocious initiation of migration (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d–f, compare with Figure 3l–o").
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of Fra upregulation in gcm GOF, supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpressing Fra in gcm KD wings is sufficient to completely reverse the migratory phenotype that results from gcm KD.
source: Second, we hypothesized that Fra may constitute an important target of Gcm in L1 glia migration and showed that overexpressing Fra in gcm KD wings is sufficient to completely reverse the migratory phenotype that results from gcm KD (Figure 6g, patterned dark blue and brown columns and Figure 6h–j).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue experiment, supported by data in Figure 6g-j.

claim: The role of the transcription factor Gcm in glial cell migration is through the direct activation of the chemoattractant receptor Fra.
source: In summary, these data suggest that the role of the transcription factor in glial cell migration is through the direct activation of the of chemoattractant receptor, Fra; this in turn implies that an early fate determinant is also capable of directly controlling late developmental events through inducing the expression of cell-surface molecules in a dose dependent manner..
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the in vitro and in vivo data showing Gcm directly regulates Fra.

claim: An early fate determinant is capable of directly controlling late developmental events through inducing the expression of cell-surface molecules in a dose dependent manner.
source: In summary, these data suggest that the role of the transcription factor in glial cell migration is through the direct activation of the of chemoattractant receptor, Fra; this in turn implies that an early fate determinant is also capable of directly controlling late developmental events through inducing the expression of cell-surface molecules in a dose dependent manner..
evidence: This is a broader conclusion drawn from the finding that Gcm, an early fate determinant, directly regulates Fra to control migration.

claim: Migration is not affected in NetAΔ mutant glia.
source: In this experiments, we find that while NetAΔ mutant glia do not display a defective migratory index (Figure 7a, compare gray and blue columns), migration is significantly affected in NetBΔ mutant glia (Figure 7a, compare gray and red columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of phenotype in NetA mutants, supported by data in Figure 7a.

claim: Migration is significantly affected in NetBΔ mutant glia.
source: In this experiments, we find that while NetAΔ mutant glia do not display a defective migratory index (Figure 7a, compare gray and blue columns), migration is significantly affected in NetBΔ mutant glia (Figure 7a, compare gray and red columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype in NetB mutants, supported by data in Figure 7a.

claim: Glia migration is comparable to that of wild-type glia in NetAΔ NetB/Y wings.
source: Glia migration was found to be comparable to that of wild-type glia in NetAΔ NetB/Y wings, whereas it is delayed in NetAΔ NetBTM/Y wings.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue of the NetB phenotype with wild-type NetB.

claim: Glia migration is delayed in NetAΔ NetBTM/Y wings.
source: Glia migration was found to be comparable to that of wild-type glia in NetAΔ NetB/Y wings, whereas it is delayed in NetAΔ NetBTM/Y wings.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype with membrane-tethered NetB.

claim: NetB must be secreted for proper glia migration to occur.
source: This suggests that NetB must be secreted for proper glia migration to occur (Figure 7a, compare light and dark purple columns) implying that the NetB ligand functions as a long-range guiding cue for the receptor Fra that is expressed in glial cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of wild-type and membrane-tethered NetB, supported by data in Figure 7a.

claim: The NetB ligand functions as a long-range guiding cue for the receptor Fra that is expressed in glial cells.
source: This suggests that NetB must be secreted for proper glia migration to occur (Figure 7a, compare light and dark purple columns) implying that the NetB ligand functions as a long-range guiding cue for the receptor Fra that is expressed in glial cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the requirement for secreted NetB.

claim: NP4151>UAS GFP reports NetB expression in the proximal region of the wing at 19 hAPF.
source: NP4151>UAS GFP reports NetB expression in the proximal region of the wing (19 hAPF) (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about NetB expression pattern, supported by data in Figure 7b.

claim: Knocking down NetB by crossing NP4151-Gal4 to UAS-NetB-RNAi results in a severe migration defect.
source: We therefore knocked down NetB by crossing NP4151-Gal4 to UAS-NetB-RNAi (NetB KD) flies and uncovered a severe migration defect, which could be rescued by simultaneously expressing UAS-NetB and UAS-NetB-RNAi (Figure 7c, first three columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the NetB knockdown phenotype, supported by data in Figure 7c.

claim: The NetB knockdown phenotype can be rescued by simultaneously expressing UAS-NetB and UAS-NetB-RNAi.
source: We therefore knocked down NetB by crossing NP4151-Gal4 to UAS-NetB-RNAi (NetB KD) flies and uncovered a severe migration defect, which could be rescued by simultaneously expressing UAS-NetB and UAS-NetB-RNAi (Figure 7c, first three columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue of the NetB knockdown phenotype, supported by data in Figure 7c.

claim: Overexpressing NetB in its territory of expression enhances the efficiency of glial cell migration.
source: Moreover, overexpressing NetB in its territory of expression enhances the efficiency of glial cell migration, as revealed by the MI at 24 hAPF (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the NetB overexpression phenotype, supported by data in Figure 7d.

claim: Ectopic expression of NetB in the posterior wing compartment using engrailed-Gal4 driver does not affect the migration efficiency of glial cells.
source: By contrast, ectopic expression of NetB in the posterior wing compartment using engrailed-Gal4 driver (en>) (Hidalgo, 1994; Lawrence and Morata, 1976) or in the distal part of the wing using GMR 29F05-Gal4 (GMR 29F05>)(Pfeiffer et al., 2008) does not affect the migration efficiency of glial cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of effect of ectopic NetB expression, supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and citations.

claim: Ectopic expression of NetB in the distal part of the wing using GMR 29F05-Gal4 does not affect the migration efficiency of glial cells.
source: By contrast, ectopic expression of NetB in the posterior wing compartment using engrailed-Gal4 driver (en>) (Hidalgo, 1994; Lawrence and Morata, 1976) or in the distal part of the wing using GMR 29F05-Gal4 (GMR 29F05>)(Pfeiffer et al., 2008) does not affect the migration efficiency of glial cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of effect of ectopic NetB expression, supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and citations.

claim: NetA is almost ubiquitously expressed in the epithelium, as revealed by the use of the Gal4 transgenic line NP4012.
source: Finally, NetA is almost ubiquitously expressed in the epithelium, as revealed by the use of the Gal4 transgenic line NP4012 (Figure 7e) (Timofeev et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2002)
evidence: This is a direct statement about NetA expression pattern, supported by data in Figure 7e and citations.

claim: Knocking down or overexpressing NetA with NP4012 driver has no impact on glia migration at early or at late stages.
source: and knocking down or overexpressing NetA with that driver has no impact on glia migration at early or at late stages (Figure 7f,g).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of effect of NetA manipulation on migration, supported by data in Figure 7f,g.

claim: NetA overexpression in the NetB expression territory fails to enhance migration efficiency.
source: Moreover, NetA overexpression in the NetB expression territory fails to enhance migration efficiency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b) or to rescue the NetB KD phenotype confirming our finding that NetA is not involved in the process of glial cell migration (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the inability of NetA to substitute for NetB, supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NetA overexpression fails to rescue the NetB KD phenotype.
source: Moreover, NetA overexpression in the NetB expression territory fails to enhance migration efficiency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b) or to rescue the NetB KD phenotype confirming our finding that NetA is not involved in the process of glial cell migration (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the inability of NetA to rescue NetB loss, supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Secreted NetB in the proximal wing provides a crucial chemoattractant cue for Gcm-mediated Fra expression, hence controlling the efficiency of glia migration.
source: Altogether, our data strongly support the hypothesis that secreted NetB in the proximal wing provides a crucial chemoattractant cue for Gcm-mediated Fra expression, hence controlling the efficiency of glia migration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the NetB expression, loss-of-function, and gain-of-function data.

claim: NetB may contribute but is not sufficient to trigger directionality of glia migration.
source: Our data also suggest that NetB may contribute but is not sufficient to trigger directionality.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that ectopic NetB does not redirect migration.

claim: unc5 has been previously shown to be transiently expressed and required in the embryonic exit and peripheral glia associated with both the segmental and intersegmental nerves.
source: unc5 is a repellant receptor for Netrins and has been previously shown to be transiently expressed and required in the embryonic exit and peripheral glia (PG) associated with both the segmental and intersegmental nerves (von Hilchen et al., 2010; Keleman and Dickson, 2001; Freeman et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a direct statement about previous findings on unc5, supported by citations.

claim: Unc5 is undetectable in the wing disc at 15 hAPF.
source: Unc5 is undetectable in the wing disc at 15 hAPF (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a–a").
evidence: This is a direct statement about Unc5 expression timing, supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unc5 expression is first seen at 18 hAPF at low levels and this expression progressively decreases to completely fade away by 29 hAPF.
source: Its expression is first seen at 18 hAPF at low levels and this expression progressively decreases to completely fade away by 29 hAPF (Figure 8a–d''').
evidence: This is a direct statement about Unc5 expression dynamics, supported by data in Figure 8a-d.

claim: Neither RNAi-mediated KD of unc5, nor the null unc58 mutation affect glia migration efficiency at the early and late stages of development.
source: If unc5 were to act as a repulsive receptor, the efficiency of glia migration would increase if its expression decreases, but neither RNAi-mediated KD of unc5, nor the null unc58 mutation (Labrador et al., 2005) affect glia migration efficiency at the early and late stages of development (Figure 8e, first three columns; Figure 8—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of phenotype in unc5 loss-of-function, supported by data in Figure 8e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1b, and citation.

claim: Overexpressing Unc5 affects the efficiency of glia migration by delaying it.
source: We then asked whether Unc5 expression must be tightly regulated, and found that overexpressing Unc5 affects the efficiency of glia migration by delaying it, a phenotype that is opposite to the Fra overexpression phenotype (Figure 8e, compare blank and green columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the unc5 overexpression phenotype, supported by data in Figure 8e.

claim: The delayed migration phenotype caused by unc5 overexpression is rescued by reducing the levels of unc5 using the unc5 KD construct or the mutant allele unc58.
source: This delayed migration phenotype was rescued by reducing the levels of unc5 using the unc5 KD construct or the mutant allele unc58, in this overexpression background. This rescue demonstrates a direct effect of unc5 on glia migration (Figure 8e, patterned green and purple column, Figure 8—figure supplement 1c, third column).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue of the unc5 overexpression phenotype, supported by data in Figure 8e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1c.

claim: fra and unc5 serve opposite roles in glia migration, with fra being necessary to trigger migration and unc5 delaying the migratory process.
source: Thus, fra and unc5 serve opposite roles in glia migration, with fra being necessary to trigger migration and unc5 delaying the migratory process.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the opposite effects of fra and unc5 on migration.

claim: The two molecules fra and unc5 seem to work in the same signaling pathway.
source: The two molecules seem to work in the same signaling pathway because the unc5 GOF phenotype is further enhanced by lowering the levels of Fra (Figure 8e, patterned green and light blue column).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic interaction between fra and unc5, supported by data in Figure 8e.

claim: The migratory phenotype induced by unc5 overexpression is rescued by simultaneously overexpressing Fra.
source: Also, the migratory phenotype induced by unc5 overexpression is rescued by simultaneously overexpressing Fra (the rescue was analyzed at an early stage for a better quantification; Figure 8f, patterned green and dark blue column).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue of unc5 overexpression by fra overexpression, supported by data in Figure 8f.

claim: Knocking down unc5 rescues the fra KD phenotype.
source: Finally, knocking down unc5 rescues the fra KD phenotype (Figure 8—figure supplement 1c, last two columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rescue of fra knockdown by unc5 knockdown, supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Unc5 can act as a repellant but its expression is not sufficient to affect migration efficiency, which is mostly controlled by Net–Fra interaction.
source: Altogether, the data described above strongly suggest that Unc5 can act as a repellant but that its expression is not sufficient to affect migration efficiency, which is mostly controlled by Net–Fra interaction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the unc5 loss-of-function and gain-of-function data.

claim: Unc5 contributes at late migratory stages.
source: A likely explanation for these results is that Unc5 contributes at late migratory stages, and time-lapse movies indeed show that unc5 overexpression delays migration but does not affect the initiation step (Figure 9—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from time-lapse analysis, supported by data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Knocking down Unc5 using repo-Gal4 results in an acceleration in migration completion.
source: To further test this hypothesis, we assessed the effects of knocking down Unc5 using repo-Gal4, which is a late glial driver compared to gcm-Gal4. In these conditions, we did see an acceleration in migration completion (Figure 8g).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype of late unc5 knockdown, supported by data in Figure 8g.

claim: Unc5 has been identified in microarrays obtained upon overexpressing Gcm.
source: Finally, since Unc5 has been identified in microarrays obtained upon overexpressing Gcm (Freeman et al. 2003) and in the DAM ID screen performed to identify the direct targets of Gcm (Cattenoz et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a direct statement about previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: Unc5 has been identified in the DAM ID screen performed to identify the direct targets of Gcm.
source: Finally, since Unc5 has been identified in microarrays obtained upon overexpressing Gcm (Freeman et al. 2003) and in the DAM ID screen performed to identify the direct targets of Gcm (Cattenoz et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the DAM ID screen results, supported by citation.

claim: Co-transfection assays in S2 cells suggest that Unc5 is a rather weak target of Gcm.
source: we asked whether Unc5 expression is directly induced by Gcm. Co-transfection assays in S2 cells similar to those performed on fra and using an Unc5–GFP reporter containing two GBS close to the unc5 transcription start site, suggest that Unc5 is a rather weak target of Gcm (Figure 8—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cell transfection assay results, supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Apart from a role for chemoattraction mediated through Fra and NetB, which determines the initiation of glial cell migration, a later chemorepulsion mediated through Fra-Unc5 ensures the termination of migration.
source: In summary, these data suggest that apart from a role for chemoattraction mediated through Fra and NetB, which determines the initiation of glial cell migration, a later chemorepulsion mediated through Fra-Unc5 ensures the termination of migration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the temporal and functional analysis of Fra, NetB, and Unc5.

claim: The expression of Unc5 is directly regulated by the transcription factor gcm.
source: Furthermore, the expression of Unc5 is also directly regulated by the transcription factor gcm suggesting that the same early determinant controls the timely expression of effector genes that initiate and terminate glial cell migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DAM ID screen and cell transfection assays.

claim: The same early determinant gcm controls the timely expression of effector genes that initiate and terminate glial cell migration.
source: Furthermore, the expression of Unc5 is also directly regulated by the transcription factor gcm suggesting that the same early determinant controls the timely expression of effector genes that initiate and terminate glial cell migration.
evidence: This is a broader conclusion about the role of Gcm in controlling multiple stages of migration.

claim: The chemoattractant receptor Fra controls glia migration in response to a long-distance signal, the chemoattractant NetB.
source: The chemoattractant receptor Fra controls glia migration in response to a long-distance signal, thechemoattractant NetB.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings regarding Fra and NetB.

claim: Fra is expressed before glia start to move and triggers migration initiation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Fra is expressed before glia start to move and triggers migration initiation in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings on Fra expression and function.

claim: Such tight control of Fra expression depends upon the Gcm transcription factor, which directly induces the expression of Fra at threshold levels.
source: Such tight control of Fra expression depends upon the Gcm transcription factor, which directly induces the expression of Fra at threshold levels.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings on Gcm regulation of Fra.

claim: The glial determinant factor also affects a specific step of collective migration by regulating the key effector gene.
source: Thus, the glial determinant factor also affects a specific step of collective migration by regulating the key effector gene.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the role of Gcm in migration.

claim: Defective glia migration is associated with several human diseases including glial brain tumors and defective regeneration following injury in the nervous system.
source: Defective glia migration is associated with several human diseases including glial brain tumors and defective regeneration following injury in the nervous system (Klämbt, 2009; Kocsis and Waxman, 2007; Oudega and Xu, 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the clinical relevance of glia migration, supported by citations.

claim: A thorough understanding of the molecules involved in the process of glia migration may contribute to the development of therapeutics for pathologies associated with defective glia migration.
source: Hence, a thorough understanding of the molecules involved in the process of glia migration may contribute to the development of therapeutics for these pathologies.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential translational impact of the research.

claim: Research progress in recent years has revealed the involvement of chemotropic cues in glia migration.
source: Research progress in recent years has revealed the involvement of chemotropic cues in glia migration (von Hilchen et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2010; Spassky et al., 2002; Kinrade et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the state of the field, supported by citations.

claim: Netrins have been described as chemotropic guidance cues for axons and migrating cells during neural development.
source: Netrins, a class of secreted laminin-related extracellular proteins, have been described as chemotropic guidance cues for axons and migrating cells during neural development (Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011; Harris et al., 1996; Ishii et al., 1992; Kennedy et al., 1994; Mitchell et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the known role of Netrins, supported by citations.

claim: In vertebrates, Netrins secreted by the floor plate cells act differentially on the migrating oligodendrocyte precursor cells and this differential outcome is dependant upon the type of receptors expressed in the migrating cells.
source: In vertebrates, Netrins secreted by the floor plate cells act differentially on the migrating oligodendrocyte precursor cells and this differential outcome is dependant upon the type of receptors expressed in the migrating cells (Spassky et al., 2002; Wolf and Friedl, 2009; Jarjour, 2003; Tsai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Netrin function in vertebrates, supported by citations.

claim: Netrins act as chemoattractants through the DCC/Frazzled family of receptors.
source: Netrins act as chemoattractants through the DCC/Frazzled family of receptors (von Hilchen et al., 2010; Lai Wing Sun et al., 2011; Chan et al., 1996; Keino-Masu et al., 1996; Kolodziej et al., 1996; Timofeev et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a direct statement about Netrin receptor function, supported by citations.

claim: Netrins act as chemorepellants through the Unc5 receptor family.
source: and chemorepellants through the Unc5 receptor family (Keleman and Dickson, 2001; Labrador et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Netrin receptor function, supported by citations.

claim: In Drosophila, the two Netrins (NetA and NetB) and their receptor Frazzled (Fra) mediate the attraction of embryonic longitudinal glia toward the midline.
source: In Drosophila, the two Netrins (NetA and NetB [Harris et al., 1996; Mitchell et al., 1996; Keleman and Dickson, 2001]) and their receptor Frazzled (Fra) mediate the attraction of embryonic longitudinal glia toward the midline (von Hilchen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Netrin function in Drosophila embryos, supported by citations.

claim: The transcriptional control underlying chemoattraction and the impact of this pathway remain largely unknown.
source: Despite the extensive knowledge on these ligands and receptors, the transcriptional control underlying chemoattraction and the impact of this pathway remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: This is the first report showing that a fate determinant directly controls collective cell migration.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report showing that a fate determinant directly controls collective cell migration, prompting us to revisit the role and mode of action of these types of molecules during development.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The cytoplasmic tail of Fra is known to play a major role in mediating Fra-dependent attractive responses in vivo and in cell culture studies.
source: The cytoplasmic tail of Fra is known to play a major role in mediating Fra-dependent attractive responses in vivo and in cell culture studies (Bashaw and Goodman, 1999; Hong et al., 1999; Ming et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the known function of the Fra cytoplasmic domain, supported by citations.

claim: A transgenic construct that lacks the Fra intracellular cytoplasmic domain was previously described as a dominant negative mutation.
source: A transgenic construct that lacks the Fra intracellular cytoplasmic domain was previously described as a dominant negative mutation (Garbe et al., 2007)
evidence: This is a direct statement about a previously characterized reagent, supported by citation.

claim: The expression of the Fra dominant negative reporter significantly reduces migration efficiency.
source: and indeed the expression of this reporter significantly reduces migration efficiency (Figure 3a, compare white and green-gray columns).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype of the dominant negative construct, supported by data in Figure 3a.

claim: Reducing Fra levels delays migration initiation.
source: To clarify why the migratory efficiency decreases in fra KD animals, we performed time-lapse analysis and found that reducing the levels of Fra affects the first step of migration (initiation), as glia start to migrate later than the control chain (Figure 3i, compare the initiation step of white and light blue columns and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the effect of fra knockdown on migration timing, supported by time-lapse data in Figure 3i and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: fra-overexpressing glia start migrating earlier than control glia, indicating that the phenotype is due to precocious initiation.
source: Accordingly, fra-overexpressing glia start migrating earlier than control glia, indicating that the phenotype is due to precocious initiation (Figure 3i–k, compare the initiation step of white and dark blue columns)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the effect of fra overexpression on migration timing, supported by time-lapse data in Figure 3i-k.

claim: Precocious initiation in fra GOF glia is associated with precocious Fra accumulation compared to that in control glia.
source: and that this is associated with precocious Fra accumulation in fra GOF glial cells compared to that in control glia (Figure 3l–o").
evidence: This is a direct statement about the correlation between Fra levels and migration timing, supported by data in Figure 3l-o.

claim: The live imaging data demonstrates that the speed of migration at the time of initiation is not higher in fra GOF glia than in control glia.
source: Finally, the live imaging data demonstrates that the speed of migration at the time of initiation is not higher in fra GOF glia than in control glia, showing that the observed phenotype is due to precocious initiation rather than to acceleration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the speed of migration, supported by time-lapse data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Repo may play a regulatory role in the maintenance of fra at late migratory stages.
source: Being a major Gcm target, repo represents a potential candidate. Our in vivo and cell transfection data using a Repo expression vector are in line with this hypothesis and suggest that Repo may play a regulatory role in the maintenance of fra at late migratory stages (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cell transfection data in Figure 9a.

claim: Repo expression first depends on Gcm but subsequently becomes independent of it through autoregulation.
source: It is known that Repo expression first depends on Gcm but subsequently becomes independent of it through autoregulation (Flici et al., 2014), indicating a transition from early to late events in gliogenesis (see model in Figure 9b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Repo regulation, supported by citation and model in Figure 9b.

claim: The initial Fra expression in wing glia strictly depends on Gcm and triggers the initiation of migration.
source: We propose that the initial Fra expression in wing glia strictly depends on Gcm and triggers the initiation of migration (see the graph in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data, supported by graph in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The overexpression of Fra using the repo promoter does not induce migratory defects.
source: Accordingly, the overexpression of Fra using the repo promoter does not induce migratory defects (Figure 9c,d)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of phenotype with late fra overexpression, supported by data in Figure 9c,d.

claim: repo>fra KD wings show only modest defects in migration initiation.
source: and repo>fra KD wings show only modest defects in migration initiation (Figure 9—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phenotype of late fra knockdown, supported by data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1b.

claim: When Gcm fades away, Repo takes over in controlling Fra expression, hence affecting later phases of migration.
source: Later on, however, when Gcm fades away, Repo takes over in controlling Fra expression, hence affecting later phases of migration (Figure 9—figure supplement 1b, see model in Figure 9b).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data, supported by data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1b and model in Figure 9b.

claim: The unc5 repellant is a weak target of Gcm that may require Repo and controls migration completion.
source: Conversely, the unc5 repellant is a weak target of Gcm thatmay require Repo and controls migration completion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the weak Gcm regulation of unc5 and its late function.

claim: The migration of embryonic longitudinal glial cells seems to rely on very early expression of Fra, which is detected in the longitudinal glial precursor, but no longer in the longitudinal glial cells.
source: With respect to what has previously been described in embryonic glia migration, we propose a different role for Netrins and their receptors in the migration of L1 glia. The migration of embryonic longitudinal glial cells seems to rely on very early expression of Fra, which is detected in the longitudinal glial precursor, but no longer in the longitudinal glial cells (von Hilchen et al., 2010; Kolodziej et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in embryonic glia, supported by citations.

claim: Fra is detected in the wing glia.
source: In our work, we do detect Fra expression in the wing glia.
evidence: This is a statement contrasting the current findings with previous work.

claim: In the case of the longitudinal glia both Netrins guide the glia toward the midline, whereas the L1 glia seem to require only NetB.
source: However, while in the case of the longitudinal glia both Netrins guide the glia toward the midline, the L1 glia seem to require only NetB.
evidence: This is a statement contrasting the current findings with previous work on embryonic glia.

claim: Ectopic expression of Netrin affects the migration of the longitudinal glia, whereas it does not do so in wing glia.
source: Moreover, ectopic expression of Netrin affects the migration of the longitudinal glia, whereas it does not do so in wing glia, hence suggesting that Netrin has a role in migration efficiency rather than on directionality.
evidence: This is a statement contrasting the current findings with previous work on embryonic glia.

claim: Netrin has a role in migration efficiency rather than on directionality in wing glia.
source: Moreover, ectopic expression of Netrin affects the migration of the longitudinal glia, whereas it does not do so in wing glia, hence suggesting that Netrin has a role in migration efficiency rather than on directionality.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of effect of ectopic Netrin on wing glia migration.

claim: Fra and Unc5 act in different migratory phases of the same glial population, the first phase being under the direct control of the Gcm glial determinant.
source: And finally, we propose that Fra and Unc5 act in different migratory phases of the same glial population, the first phase being under the direct control of the Gcm glial determinant.
evidence: This is a summary of the proposed model based on the findings.

claim: The ligand NetB is expressed early during wing development.
source: Overall, this paper displays a model in which the ligand NetB is expressed early during wing development (Figure 7—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a statement about NetB expression timing, supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fra is expressed right before migration onset and cell autonomously decides the time of migration initiation of the glial chain.
source: whereas its receptor Fra is expressed right before migration onset and cell autonomously decides the time of migration initiation of the glial chain.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings on Fra expression and function.

claim: Unc5 appears later and contributes to migration termination.
source: Unc5 appears later and contributes to migration termination.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings on Unc5 expression and function.

claim: The acquisition of the Fra levels that trigger migration is part of the cell-specification program dictated by the Gcm glial determinant.
source: The acquisition of the Fra levels that trigger migration is part of the cell-specification program dictated by the Gcm glial determinant, which not only induces the expression of downstream transcription factors but also directly implements a specific developmental program by triggering the expression of effector genes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the role of Gcm in the developmental program.

claim: Gcm not only induces the expression of downstream transcription factors but also directly implements a specific developmental program by triggering the expression of effector genes.
source: The acquisition of the Fra levels that trigger migration is part of the cell-specification program dictated by the Gcm glial determinant, which not only induces the expression of downstream transcription factors but also directly implements a specific developmental program by triggering the expression of effector genes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the dual role of Gcm.

claim: The dynamic and coordinated action of fate determinants and chemotropic cues contribute to the timely and efficient migration of the glial cells.
source: Together, these findings in the Drosophila wing suggest that the dynamic and coordinated action of fate determinants and chemotropic cues contribute to the timely and efficient migration of the glial cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: A similar molecular mechanism, relying on Netrins or other localized attractive cues and their receptors, may be used in other cases of collective migration.
source: A similar molecular mechanism, relying on Netrins or other localized attractive cues and their receptors, may be used in other cases of collective migration.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.
